title: Generalist method to reconstruct metabolic networks from multi-omics data at large-scale
summary: Metabolic network databases often suffer from inconsistent pathways with blocked reactions. Furthermore, current reconstruction methods lack scalable ways to integrate multi-omics data and cannot flexibly combine diverse modeling pipelines. We introduce SPECTRA, a unified platform that reconstructs metabolic networks across multiple biological scales. SPECTRA uses distinct optimization formulations and achieves a 56-fold speed improvement over existing algorithms for flux consistency based model reconstruction. We demonstrated SPECTRA across three applications. First, we gap-filled 7,302 microbial reconstructions from the AGORA2 database, reducing blocked reactions from an average of 482 to 169 per model. Second, we modeled synthetic gut microbiota at the community scale with superior performance in reaction inclusion. Third, we extracted models for 1,479 cancer cell lines, capturing more cancer hallmark reactions than current methods. This framework provides a scalable and flexible approach for modeling metabolic networks, and generates testable hypotheses for machine learning applications in biology.

title: High-throughput prediction of peptide structural conformations
summary: Protein structure prediction via artificial intelligence/machine learning (AI/ML) approaches has sparked substantial research interest in structural biology. In recent work, AlphaFold2 (AF2) has been adapted for the prediction of multiple structural conformations, beyond static structures, by using multiple random seeds and subsampling the multiple sequence alignment (MSA). Research applying this specialized approach has focused on regular-sized proteins, while smaller peptides remain underexplored in this context. Here, we report AF2-based multi-conformation prediction and systematic analyses of a set of 557 peptides (10-40 residues in length) with corresponding nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) ensemble coordinates. We found that predicted ensembles varied in similarity to experimental coordinate data, with disulfide-rich peptides bearing somewhat closer resemblance whereas -helical peptides exhibited greater dissimilarity. Distinct correlations involving MSA depth were also observed. These results reveal notable capabilities of AF2-based multi-conformation prediction for peptides but also highlight considerable limitations, emphasizing the need for interpretation discretion and improved multi-conformation prediction approaches.

title: Constructing Gene Regulatory Network using Chatterjee's Rank Correlation with Single-cell Transcriptomic Data
summary: Constructing gene regulatory networks (GRNs) from single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) data is critical for understanding cellular systems, yet existing methods rely either on strong modeling assumptions or on computationally intensive algorithms. We introduce a multiple testing framework for GRN construction based on Chatterjee's rank correlation coefficient, a nonparametric measure of dependence that captures non-linear and non-monotone relationships. The framework overcomes several limitations of traditional methods by offering a transparent, scalable, and computationally efficient alternative to recent black-box machine learning models. Because cells in scRNA-seq data are not independent observations, we develop a data-driven algorithm for estimating robust testing cutoffs. We further exploit the asymmetric nature of Chatterjee's correlation to propose a new test for asymmetric predictive associations, yielding biologically meaningful and directionally informed GRNs. In simulations, our method matches or outperforms state-of-the-art approaches in recovering true gene-gene dependencies and asymmetric associations, particularly for complex, non-linear dependencies. Application to real scRNA-seq data shows its utility for dissecting complex regulatory networks.

title: Molecular and phenotypic footprints of climate in native Arabidopsis thaliana
summary: Climate change poses a major threat to humanity by driving biodiversity loss and reducing crop yields. To understand the molecular and developmental impacts of rising temperatures, plant science has relied heavily on the model organism Arabidopsis thaliana. Despite decades of research, its development under fully natural conditions remains poorly understood, and only approximately 30% of A. thaliana genes have experimental functional annotations, probably because many functions are subtle or manifest only in specific laboratory or ecological contexts. Here, we address this gap with a landscape transcriptomic approach that integrates intensive phenotyping and transcriptomic profiling of naturally occurring plants in their native habitats. Across two field sites sampled between 2021 and 2025, we collected >30,000 quantitative trait measurements from more than 3,000 A. thaliana plants and generated >1,600 matching transcriptomes. Together with population genomic analyses indicating limited within-population genetic diversity, these data provide an opportunity to investigate phenotypic and transcriptional plasticity associated with natural climatic fluctuations. Year-to-year variation in weather, including temperature anomalies, was associated with differences in plant traits, and climatic variables together explained up to 17% of phenotypic variation. In situ transcriptomes carried clear temperature and local environmental signatures, closely matching temperature-response programs known from the laboratory. Leveraging paired per-plant transcriptomes and phenotypes, we applied machine learning to predict regulators of climate-relevant and other plant traits under natural conditions. The models recovered canonical thermomorphogenesis regulators, including PHYTOCHROME INTERACTING FACTOR 4 (PIF4), providing ecological evidence that temperature signaling pathways defined in controlled environments operate in the wild, and expanded this regulatory landscape by identifying hormonal receptors, signaling components, and previously uncharacterized genes, some of which we functionally validated. Together, this work demonstrates that landscape transcriptomics, by pairing field transcriptomes capturing environmental and regulatory states with phenotypes, enables the predictive identification of genetic regulators of temperature responses and broader plant traits. This makes landscape transcriptomics a scalable framework for climate-aware functional genomics in plants.

title: EvoRx: Machine Learning-Based Prediction of Antibiotic Resistance in Escherichia coli Using Genomic Features
summary: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) complicates bacterial infection management, motivating genomic approaches to predicting antibiotic susceptibility. This study assessed the predictive performance and generalisability of machine-learning models using resistance-associated genomic features from Escherichia coli. Publicly available genomic and phenotypic records yielded 446 genomes, 252 binary genomic features and 1,935 susceptibility observations across nine antibiotics. Logistic Regression, Random Forest and XGBoost classifiers were compared using validation ROC-AUC, followed by evaluation on held-out test subsets. Additional analyses examined identical genomic feature profiles across partitions, performance across source publications and feature redundancy. Ampicillin and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole achieved held-out accuracies of 93.98% and 93.59%, ROC-AUC values of 0.912 and 0.954, and resistant-isolate recall of 95.16% and 94.55%, respectively. In contrast, ceftazidime achieved 88.52% accuracy and 0.940 ROC-AUC but identified only 22.22% of resistant isolates. Seventy-four held-out observations shared identical 252-feature profiles with training isolates; all were correctly classified. After excluding overlapping observations without retraining, ROC-AUC decreased from 0.912 to 0.848 for ampicillin and from 0.954 to 0.901 for trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole. Exploratory cross-publication evaluations showed variable performance, with shared multilocus sequence types in 16 of 18 comparisons. Reducing genomic features did not materially alter validation performance in the two antibiotics examined. These findings indicate that genomic predictors can discriminate resistance phenotypes, but aggregate accuracy may obscure poor resistant-isolate detection. The findings also distinguish performance on conventionally held-out isolates from performance on previously unseen resistance-feature profiles, an important consideration when bacterial population structure and correlated determinants substantially influence model evaluation. Independent phylogenetic and prospective validation remains necessary before clinical use.

title: Wilson disease mechanisms manipulate ATP7B activity
summary: Copper is an essential cofactor for enzymes involved in diverse processes including mitochondrial respiration and the metabolism of neurotransmitters, collagen and melanin. However, its redox activity requires tight homeostatic control. The P-type ATPases ATP7A and ATP7B help deliver copper to cuproenzymes, and ATP7B mediates the excretion of excess copper into bile. Pathogenic ATP7B variants cause Wilson disease (WD), leading to copper accumulation in organs including the liver, kidney, and brain, and to disruption of copper-dependent processes. Current treatments primarily reduce systemic copper levels, while emerging gene therapies aim to restore ATP7B function. A complementary therapeutic strategy would be to rescue dysfunctional ATP7B using pharmacological chaperones, but their development is limited by an insufficient understanding of how WD variants perturb ATP7B structure and function. Here, we present a cryo-EM structure of human ATP7B reconstituted in lipid nanodiscs together with coarse-grained molecular dynamics simulations, as well as mutagenesis, functional and sequence analyses. We identify a salt bridge (E754-R969), crucial for the transition between inward- and outward-facing conformations, which is abolished by the R969Q disease variant. Additionally, we find a conserved stabilizing cholesterol-binding site severely disrupted by the WD variant W939C. Furthermore, we present new insights into the dynamics of metal binding domains 5 and 6 hinting at a copper relay mechanism in ATP7B. Together, these findings reveal lipid- and domain-mediated mechanisms of ATP7B regulation and explain how specific WD variants disrupt them, providing a structural framework for mutation-directed therapeutic strategies, including pharmacological chaperones.

title: Host HSP90 mimicry by a parasite effector triggers mitochondrial membrane shedding
summary: The outer mitochondrial membrane mediates critical host defenses against intracellular pathogens. How microbes manipulate this compartment remains poorly understood. Here, we found that the human parasite Toxoplasma gondii remodels host mitochondrial membranes through molecular mimicry of HSP90 chaperones. Cryo-electron microscopy analyses showed that the parasite effector TgMAF1 binds the same specialized clamp domain of the mitochondrial import receptor TOM70 as chaperones of the HSP70/90 family. Biochemical and comparative genomics analyses demonstrate that this mimicry arose through the neofunctionalization of the TgMAF1 C-terminus from an ancestral paralog incapable of TOM70 binding. In molecular dynamics simulations, complexed TgMAF1-TOM70 triggered the formation of higher order assemblies that induced local membrane curvature. These findings uncover a previously unknown host subversion strategy and establish molecular mimicry of a chaperone as a mechanism for pathogen-driven remodeling of the host OMM.

title: Detection of Melanoma Using Deep Serum Proteome Profiling and Machine Learning
summary: Background Early detection is the primary determinant of melanoma survival yet screening still relies on visual inspection and no serum protein biomarkers are in clinical use for early detection We sought to identify serum protein signatures of melanoma development in a longitudinal military cohort Methods Using the Department of Defense Serum Repository we analyzed 390 serum samples from 73 melanoma cases and 73 matched controls collected at up to four timepoints spanning 4 years before to 2 years after diagnosis Samples were profiled by data independent acquisition mass spectrometry with nanoparticle based protein enrichment Proteins were filtered using a signal to noise metric derived from pooled quality control samples Random forest classifiers with leave one out cross validation univariate pre filtering and Boruta feature selection were applied to cross sectional case control and longitudinal within subject comparisons Performance was assessed by the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve and models were compared using DeLongs test Results We quantified 3364 proteins Cross sectional classification in the diagnosis window of 1 year or less post diagnosis reached an area under the curve of 0823 with a 95 percent confidence interval of 0723 to 0923 driven by an eight protein consensus signature PRSS1 GSK3B FAM20C CES1 CCL14 EPHA10 LMAN2 ITIH1 spanning proteases immune activation and extracellular matrix remodeling Discrimination was weak before diagnosis with areas under the curve of 0609 at 2 years and 0566 at 4 years prior the latter not distinguishable from chance The serine proteases PRSS1 and PRSS2 recurred across cross sectional and longitudinal models Adding age or military service branch did not improve classification beyond proteins alone Conclusions Deep serum proteome profiling distinguishes melanoma cases from matched controls in the diagnosis window and yields candidate markers with weak signals preceding clinical diagnosis In the absence of external validation these findings provide preliminary evidence for a minimally invasive serum protein based approach to melanoma detection that could complement visual screening and help triage at risk individuals for dermatologic evaluation pending validation in larger more diverse cohorts

title: Resistome-based machine learning source attribution of a superbug
summary: Many bacterial human pathogens infect not only humans but also other species, and source attribution has been very useful for studying transmission among the different sources. Yet, critical pathogens such as Acinetobacter baumannii have not been studied using source attribution approaches. Here, we conducted machine source attribution using the resistome of almost 1200 A. baumannii genomes from four sources: humans, companion animals , soil, and white storks. Of note, no other study has used the resistome as input data before. First, we selected the best model among 168 parameter combinations, which was Random Forest, with 5-fold cross-validation and chi2 for feature selection. The model shows a reasonably good accuracy with an F1 weighted score = 0.744, yet class accuracy was dependent on the source. Whereas for companion animals and humans, 93% and 86% of the predictions were correct, respectively; the other two categories (soil and white stork) show correct predictions below 50%. Yet, a core phylogeny and ST assignment reveal that the wrong predictions are associated with multi-host lineages. Finally, we identify the most important ARGs contributing to each class prediction and, in the case of companion animals, tetgenes, which confer resistance to tetracycline, were among the top contributors. Our study shows the resistome's potential for developing models to predict source associations. More broadly, this study shows how integrating machine learning and phylogenomics can help us understand multi-host transmission dynamics.

title: Physics-Informed Modeling of Biological Aging through DNA Methylation Entropy
summary: Epigenetic clocks based on DNA methylation patterns are among the most accurate molecular correlates of chronological age, yet widely used clocks are predominantly empirical models with limited explicit characterization of the underlying methylation variability, lacking a direct connection to the physical mechanisms of aging. In this work, we bridge this gap by introducing an information-theoretic framework for DNA methylation dynamics combined with nonlinear machine learning to develop a competitive and interpretable age predictor. We model the population distribution of methylation {beta}-values at each CpG site using a reparameterized three-parameter Generalized Gamma Distribution (GGD) and derive a closed-form expression for its differential Shannon entropy. The resulting CpG-level entropy is used to characterize methylation variability and as a criterion for locus filtering. We introduce the Stacy Gradient Boosting Clock (Stacy-GB), which combines this GGD-based representation with a LightGBM regressor. The model was evaluated across independent cohorts using the ComputAgeBench epigenetic clock benchmark. Stacy-GB achieved a mean absolute error (MAE) of 3.74 years and a median error (bias) of 2.41 years, significantly outperforming state-of-the-art epigenetic clock baselines. Furthermore, age acceleration estimated by Stacy-GB was associated with several clinical pathologies, including ischemic heart disease, HIV infection, multiple sclerosis, and Werner syndrome, supporting its potential as an accurate and biophysically grounded tool for clinical aging research.

title: BI-SCUDO Regression - A novel algorithm to infer clinical variables from omics datasets
summary: Regression analysis of high-throughput omics data is often made difficult by noise, batch effects, and the loss of information resulting from the discretization of continuous variables. Existing machine learning algorithms often struggle to extract stable biological signals under these heterogeneous conditions. We introduce BI-SCUDO Regression, a rank-based regression framework designed for omics data analysis. By leveraging within-sample rankings and network-based predictions, BI-SCUDO Regression bypasses the need for complex normalization and provides robust, interpretable results. In synthetic benchmarks, BI-SCUDO Regression demonstrated strong resilience to noise, maintaining predictive and feature-selection stability under conditions in which standard models exhibited performance degradation. When applied to cohorts from TCGA datasets, BI-SCUDO Regression consistently outperformed LASSO, Random Forest Regression, and XGBoost in predicting survival, with an average increase in Ratio of Performance to Deviation ranging from 43% to 86%, depending on the comparator. Furthermore, the algorithm consistently identified parsimonious, statistically significant, and biologically relevant biomarkers, with enrichment for cancer-related terms across all stage stratifications. Although BI-SCUDO Regression incurs higher training times due to its genetic optimization strategy, it offers a robust and interpretable approach to outcome prediction and biomarker discovery, with potential applications in precision medicine, where noisy data compromise the performance of conventional regression methods.

title: Measuring the information budget of cross-target antibody affinity generalization: a robust cross-target wall, and why structure reaches developability but not affinity
summary: Structure-based machine learning is widely expected to advance antibody engineering, yet it is unclear how far affinity predictions transfer to new targets, and why. We introduce a noise-corrected, censoring-aware estimator of the cross-target transfer ceiling, {rho}max = {surd}(T/(T+I)), which separates a transferable antibody-intrinsic component (T) from a non-transferable target-specific interaction (I). On deterministic synthetic ground truth the estimator recovers the noise-free ceiling to {+/-} 0.0003, whereas the naive sum-of-squares estimator is biased downward by measurement noise. Applying it from synthetic to real systems, the transferable budget is small, and on real neutralization panels it is not an artefact: the target-specific interaction survives noise and censoring correction. It is strongly regime-dependent, with a two-tier structure: predicting a novel antibody from sequence alone (the design setting) reaches a lower ceiling ({rho} {approx} 0.44 on real breadth data) than ranking a characterized one ({rho} {approx} 0.59), even with a strong protein language model. Synthetic oracles also overstate transferability: an oracle scored on real predicted structures carries about half the budget of a matched synthetic lattice (0.45 vs. 0.81), and real neutralization and escape panels sit well below the synthetic ceiling (0.32-0.68). Under leakage-free antigen-cluster splits, cross-target affinity ranking across every method family collapses to this budget, while within a sampled target a structure-based graph network ranks affinity above off-the-shelf FoldX and GearBind (within-complex Spearman 0.55), and structural surface descriptors predict a surface-driven developability property (hydrophobic aggregation) where sequence-dominated properties (humanness, charge-driven self-association) do not benefit. A controlled ablation attributes the residual within-target signal to the antibody alone: dropping the antigen from the structural model leaves it essentially unchanged (interface {Delta} {rho} between -0.01 and +0.02 across four panels), so for this model the paratope-epitope interface adds no ranking signal over the antibody alone. Models climb toward the budget within a target -- via a measure-then-rank operating mode that recovers top binders 6-8 times more efficiently than random once a target has been sampled -- but none crosses it.

title: Molecular analysis of 55 dopamine transporter variants from psychiatric patients reveals convergent mechanisms of dysfunction
summary: Rare genetic variants are increasingly recognized as contributors to neuropsychiatric disease and may reveal underlying pathobiological mechanisms. The dopamine transporter (DAT), encoded by SLC6A3, regulates dopaminergic neurotransmission through rapid dopamine (DA) reuptake. Although disease-associated DAT variants have been linked to disorders ranging from infantile parkinsonism to neuropsychiatric disease, the molecular basis of DAT dysfunction remains poorly understood. Here, we systematically investigated 55 DAT missense variants identified in the iPSYCH2012-nested case-control cohort. By assessing transport activity, inhibitor binding, cell-surface expression, subcellular localization, amphetamine responsiveness and constitutive DA efflux, we resolved the variants into seven phenotypic classes. These reflected distinct molecular defects, including impaired substrate and ion coupling, destabilized intramolecular interactions, and defective folding, trafficking or surface expression. Molecular dynamics simulations provided structural insight into representative variants. Collectively, our findings reveal mechanistic convergence of genetically diverse DAT variants and establish a framework for interpreting the pathogenicity of newly identified SLC6A3 variants.

title: Modern speech recognition systems exhibit human-like word recognition but superhuman use of statistical dependencies between words
summary: Advances in machine learning have yielded machine systems that approach human performance on real-world perception tasks. For speech recognition, it remains unclear whether such models' behavior resembles that of humans. We addressed this question by measuring word recognition abilities in humans and models across 272 speech distortions, providing a detailed behavioral fingerprint. Three recent industry speech recognition models trained on hundreds of years of speech outperformed humans. However, in conditions where linguistic context was removed, they matched human performance well, suggesting that the models are superhuman in their ability to leverage statistical dependencies between words. Experiments manipulating model training data suggest that training data variability and realism contribute to the match to human perception. Overall, the results show that superhuman performance is now possible with systems that are optimized over enough data and suggest that accurate models of human speech recognition require optimization over appropriate tasks and amounts of speech.

title: Native architecture of a mitochondrial oxphosome
summary: Mitochondrial cristae are the primary bioenergetic units of eukaryotic cells, yet the molecular principles that dictate their morphologies remain largely unknown. Using in situ cryo-electron tomography and integrative modeling, we resolve the native organization of the respiratory machinery in the diatom Phaeodactylum tricornutum. Unlike previously studied animals and green algae, diatoms possess tubular crista, a conserved membrane architecture found in diverse and globally relevant species. We identify several native supercomplexes assemblies, including an oxphosome comprising the entire respiratory chain. Our results, together with molecular dynamics analyses, reveal that these supercomplexes assemble through a lipid-mediated mechanism. We propose that tubular cristae are shaped by the interplay between membrane-bending ATP synthase oligomers that bud the hemispherical crista tips and supercomplexes that act as molecular roadblocks to constrain ATP synthase propagation, thereby balancing membrane curvature and allowing cristae body extension. Furthermore, we show that the diatom Complex I retains ancestral subunits related to fatty acid synthase. Beyond illuminating diatom bioenergetics, our findings reveal a fundamental principle of mitochondrial morphogenesis where ATP synthase-driven membrane curvature is spatially fine-tuned by respiratory supercomplexes.
